item.title: Did Trump know Musk was about to restrict Ukraine’s military Starlink service? WSJ reports they discussed the decision afterward. Some sources say they also spoke beforehand.
item.description: SpaceX founder Elon Musk ordered restrictions on Ukraine’s use of Starshield, the military version of the Starlink satellite communications system, sources told The Wall Street Journal.
item.content:encoded:
SpaceX founder Elon Musk ordered restrictions on Ukraine’s use of Starshield, the military version of the Starlink satellite communications system, sources told The Wall Street Journal.

The sources said Musk’s decision caused “panic in Kyiv” and “confusion inside the Trump administration.”

As the uproar grew, SpaceX representatives contacted their White House counterparts to agree on a statement saying the company and the Trump administration had coordinated their actions.

Musk and Trump discussed the decision by phone shortly after the Starlink restrictions became public, two sources told The Wall Street Journal. One source said Musk and Trump had also discussed the issue before the decision to impose restrictions.

Some officials say Musk acted unilaterally and Trump gave no specific order. But a source familiar with the situation said Musk had spoken with several senior administration officials, including Trump, before imposing the restrictions.

On October 14, Ukrainian forces reported restrictions on their Starlink satellite communications terminals — specifically, the military version, Starshield. The restrictions disrupted Ukrainian military missions, among other things.

Two days later, Trump said he had not ordered restrictions on Starshield in Ukraine and did not know who could have done so. But The Telegraph, citing four sources, reported that Musk had approached Trump with a proposal to limit Starlink speeds in Ukraine. One of the newspaper’s sources said Trump agreed.

Ukraine’s military Starlink access

  • How Ukraine’s military uses Starlink — and what would happen if the Trump administration cut off its satellite communications entirely
  • Ukrainian troops lost Starlink access for a day. Elon Musk and the Trump White House both deny responsibility.

item.title: Trump says Putin and Zelensky don’t need to meet face to face to reach a peace deal
item.description: Donald Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff could “pave the way for a meeting at leaders’ level” during talks with Vladimir Putin, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said at a news conference in Oslo.
item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff could “pave the way for a meeting at leaders’ level” during talks with Vladimir Putin, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said at a news conference in Oslo.

“Steve Witkoff will fly tomorrow to St. Petersburg where he will be meeting with Russian leadership and exchange ideas from this meeting and the proposals that have been worked on by European and American colleagues, and possibly pave the way for a meeting at leaders’ level,” Støre said.

Politico reported, without quoting Støre directly, that Witkoff would offer Putin direct talks with Trump and Zelensky.

Zelensky said after meeting Witkoff in Oslo that “one of the important ideas is to move to a potential trilateral meeting of the leaders to address the issues that only the leaders can do.” “Steve is going to Russia tomorrow, and let’s see what Putin has to say,” Zelensky added.

When reporters asked Trump whether Putin and Zelensky needed to “be in the same room” to reach a peace agreement, he said: “I mean, [it] depends. They don’t have to be in the same room. I guess I can do it another way. It’s hard for them to be in the same room. I don’t care how it’s done.”

Russia–Ukraine peace talks

  • U.S. pushes to revive Ukraine–Russia talks after Witkoff and Kushner meet Zelensky in Kyiv
  • Europe is preparing for direct talks with Putin, FT reports. One possible proposal: Russia gets Donbas, Ukraine gets NATO membership.

item.title: Poland orders four Russians and 11 Belarusians to leave after they enter on tourist visas, apparently hoping to compete at a world karate championship
item.description: Polish Border Guard officers detained 15 Russian and Belarusian citizens who apparently intended to compete in the world karate championships for youth, junior, and under-21 athletes in Bielsko-Biała.
item.content:encoded:
Polish Border Guard officers detained 15 Russian and Belarusian citizens who apparently intended to compete in the world karate championships for youth, junior, and under-21 athletes in Bielsko-Biała.

The detainees — 11 Belarusians and four Russians — entered Poland on tourist visas, which, according to Border Guard spokesperson Szymon Mościcki, “did not match the stated purpose of their stay.” All were ordered to leave the country within eight days.

The karate championships took place from September 14 to 18. Polish authorities had barred Russian athletes from the outset. The Russian Karate Federation said it “had anticipated this situation and therefore had not recommended that anyone take part in this tournament,” but also “could not stand in the way of the athletes’ own wishes” to compete in the event.

The organizers said no Russian athletes had registered by the deadline. As early as October 8, the Polish Karate Union said the Russians would not be coming. Piotr Borys, Poland’s deputy minister of sport and tourism, said Poland had a firm policy of barring Russian athletes from competitions in the country.

The organizers nevertheless expected Russians to try to take part in the tournament. “That’s why we warned them in advance through our contacts in the sport not to come,” said Polish Karate Union President Paweł Połtorzecki.

The Russian Karate Federation said it knew about the ban and that the athletes had been expelled because they “entered on visas that did not cover the purpose of their visit.” “We knew this was how it would turn out. That’s why no one from the federation went,” it said.

The Russians being expelled from Poland have not been named. The news outlet Vot Tak reported that students at the Oryol-Karat school were among those who wanted to attend the competition. The school’s administrators send aid to Russian troops and organize meetings between children and people who have taken part in the war.
